newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Plan to sell USS Maine cemetery plot angers Key West.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Plan to sell USS Maine cemetery plot angers Key West.

text.p: Remember the Maine! With that war cry U.S. troops charged into the Spanish-American War vowing to avenge the 260 sailors who died in the explosion of the battleship Maine in Havana harbour on Feb.15, 1898.

Now angry Key West residents say the U.S. Navy is discarding the Maine's dead just as the centennial nears of the war that launched the United States as an imperial power. A Navy-owned plot in the city cemetery with the graves of 24 Maine sailors has been deemed "excess" to Navy needs and Naval Air Station Key West is trying to get rid of it.

"I feel it's a very sad situation that our military planners consider American heroes in excess," Joe Pais, vice chairman of the USS Battleship Maine Centennial Commission, told Reuters. "The plot should stand as a tribute to those who served this country."

A statue of a sailor clutching an oar looks over the graves, proudly saluting his comrades from the Maine buried in the fenced-off plot, 17 of whom are anonymous. In all the plot holds the remains of 171 servicemen, most of whom died in the Civil War. Four perished in an attack on the torpedo boat Winslow in the Spanish-American war. There are also two British Royal Navy officers killed in a car crash in 1951.
Key West, at the end of the Florida Keys island chain just 90 miles (145 km) from Havana, was the Maine's last homeport and a vital U.S. Navy base in the Spanish-American war.
MAINE EXPLOSION AN IMPORTANT FACTOR IN 1898 WAR

Although the cause of the Maine's destruction was never officially established, it was widely blamed on a Spanish mine and was an important factor in the events that led to the conflict in which Spain eventually lost Cuba, the Philippines, Puerto Rico and Guam to the United States.
"Definitely there is no intent to dishonour the dead," Lt. Jonathan Hupp, spokesman for Naval Air Station Key West, said. "We are trying to get them taken better care of."

Congress ordered the Navy to draw up a list of properties that no longer had an operational use under base closing and realignment procedures, Hupp said. "The plot has no active use. The graves are of historical significance. We are not in that business and we are not trained to look after historical sites."

Some parts of the sell-off could be lucrative for Key West. The Truman Waterfront dock has potential to be developed for cruise ships while quarters and barracks could be turned into public housing. Other historical sites are also on offer such as the Seminole Battery built in the 1890s and the Civil War-era East Martello Battery with its distinctive watchtower.
Hupp said the Navy would spend more than $50,000 to renovate the burial plot before any handover and planned a major ceremony there next year to mark the centennial.
City authorities have not made clear if they want to take over the site. Even so, the prospect leaves some unhappy.

"People are upset, expecially veterans," said Tom Hambright, a local historian who served 21 years in the Navy. He said the site should be taken over by the federal agency that runs the National Cemetery at Arlington, Virginia.
"We're all concerned about long-term preservation. The city will cut the grass but can it maintain the statue and the graves over the next 50 or 100 years?" Hambright asked.
"I don't see how it can be classified excess property," he added. "It's still in use. People are still buried there."
The issue prompted Florida Representative Pete Deutsch to write to the Navy. If no one takes over the site, the Navy will be obliged to keep it, his spokeswoman Karen Frye said.

Pais said he was particularly irked since renowned Brazilian architect Oscar Neidmeyer, who designed Brasilia, will dedicate a monument in Havana next Feb. 15 to mark what President Fidel Castro's Communist government defines as 100 years of oppression of the Cuban people by the United States.
"We're decommissioning a grave and they're raising a monument," he said. "We are negating our own history."
